title: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
answer: Testing arguments before peer review is the work an author does to stress the central claim, the supporting evidence, and the reasoning of a manuscript before it enters formal review. In AI research it covers benchmark results, dataset descriptions, statistical tests, ablation studies, and the fit between conclusions and experiments. It also includes anticipating reviewer objections, checking definitions, and separating what the data show from what the author hopes they show. This stage does not replace peer review, it makes the later review more productive by removing avoidable weaknesses.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Testing arguments before peer review is the work an author does to stress the central claim, the supporting evidence, and the reasoning of a manuscript before it enters formal review. In AI research it covers benchmark results, dataset descriptions, statistical tests, ablation studies, and the fit between conclusions and experiments. It also includes anticipating reviewer objections, checking definitions, and separating what the data show from what the author hopes they show. This stage does not replace peer review, it makes the later review more productive by removing avoidable weaknesses.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the ordinary infrastructure of research: reference managers, version control, shared document editors, experiment trackers, and reproducible notebooks. For AI papers it also depends on compute logs, dataset documentation, model cards, and code repositories that record the exact configuration behind each result. Internal review can happen in lab meetings, writing groups, or preprint comment threads, and it often uses checklists for statistics, ethics, and reproducibility. The aim is to make the argument inspectable, not to add ceremony.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common method is to restate the central claim in one sentence, then map every supporting sentence to a specific result, citation, or definition. Authors test alternative explanations, check whether baselines are fair, rerun key experiments with different seeds, and ask a colleague to write the strongest possible reviewer objection. A researcher can compare each claim with a corpus of prior claims, such as the site's 12233 extracted claims, to see whether the wording is supported, contradicted, or already known. The output is a revised manuscript, a list of remaining uncertainties, and a clear statement of what the evidence does not show.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this stage centre on provenance, attribution, and disclosure. Authors need to know the licence and consent status of every dataset, the origin of every model weight, and the contribution of every collaborator, including anyone who used generative tools. Risks include plagiarism, self-plagiarism, undisclosed conflicts, privacy breaches, and claims that outrun the evidence. Venue policies on preprints, embargoes, and AI assistance vary, so the manuscript's provenance record is part of the argument itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward earlier and more continuous scrutiny, with preprints, registered reports, and open review platforms moving critique before formal submission. Automated tools may help flag unsupported claims, missing citations, and statistical inconsistencies, but human judgment remains central to judging novelty and significance. As AI research matures, pre-review testing is likely to include more standard reporting for data, code, and models, and more routine use of claim extraction and argument mapping. The boundary between pre-review testing and peer review may blur, but the purpose stays the same: to make the argument clear enough to be tested.
